title: Latvia in International Trade
text: The culminating point of Latvia's participation in international trade was attained in 1929, in which year the turnover of our foreign trade totalled 636 million lats, the imports having involved a sum of 362 million lats, while the exports rendered only 274 millions. The balance of trade was therefore adverse to the extent of 88 million lats. Adverse returns were also registered in previous years. In 1924, for example, the imports exceeded the exports by 86.3 million lats, in 1925 by 100.9 million lats and in 1926 by 71.8 millions. Notwithstanding this unsatisfactory trend, Latvia adhered to a liberal policy of foreign trade. Moderate customs tariffs of a fiscal character were the only protective means of any importance employed. The customs tariff which was published in the official gazette „Valdibas Vestnesis" on March 30, 1928 and enforced on April 16 of the same year, still constitutes the basis of the tariff system in this country. A notable feature of the commercial treaties which Latvia concluded with almost all countries was the acceptance of the unlimited, unconditional principle of the most favoured nation — which, in keeping wTith the liberal trade regime, enhanced the development of Latvian foreign trade. The economic depression which engulfed the world naturally affected Latvia's participation in international trade. The 636 million lats foreign trade turnover of the year 1929 diminished gradually until the lowest level — 173 million lats — was reached in 1933, in which year the depression was most keenly felt in the foreign trade of this country. Conditions improved, however, in the second half of 1934 in consequence of the energetic measures adopted by the National Government of Latvia to combat the economic crisis. The result was that the turnover of foreign trade amounted to 180 million lats by the end of 1934, compared with 173 millions in the preceding year. The improvement continued in 1935, in the first nine months of which our foreign trade returns were larger than in the corresponding period of the preceding two years. The turnover of foreign trade totalled 125 million lats in the first three quarters of 1933, rose to 128.1 mill, in the following year and totalled 149.1 mill, lats last year. Thus, there was an increase of 21 mill, lats or 16.4% in 1935, compared with the corresponding period of 1934. The balance of trade in nine months of 1935 was adverse to the extent of 6.5 million lats.

title: Agriculture in Latvia
text: Farming, as a national occupation of the Latvians, dates back to ancient times, — the art of cultivating the soil having been handed down as a treasured heritage from generation to generation. The same kinds of cereals found in Latvia today were grown here 10 centuries ago when only a slightly smaller number of inhabitants subsisted on the fruits of agricultural labour. And although, in the course of centuries, the land of the Latvians was the scene of many wars in which hostile armies swept the country leaving utter desolation in their wake, Latvia has always succeeded in re-mustering her forces, restoring order and resuscitating her economic life. In spite of all setbacks, the Latvian farmer always returned with indomitable courage to the work handed down to him by his ancestors. He cultivated his fields, improved and increased his herds and maintained the high level of agricultural development peculiar to this country. Agricultural activities were intensified after the Great War and there was a rapid increase in the different crops in post-war years. The general development of the various branches of agriculture has been enhanced since then by successful propaganda and the enforcement of regulations governing the trade in agricultural produce. The fact that the average crop per hectare in the last three years surpassed the pre-war yield by 30— 40% is due not only to intensive work and the use of better seeds, but also to the employment of rational methods of farming and the institution of a well organised system of agronomical assistance. The steady development of farming in the last three years was greatly enhanced by the establishing of the Latvian Chamber of Agriculture, which is one of the factors of the Chamber system devised and realised by the National Government of Latvia. The Chamber of Agriculture replaces the numerous organisations which existed formerly for the purpose of promoting agriculture. The object of the Chamber is not only to promote agriculture, but also to further and represent the interests of agricultural circles in Latvia, at the same time encouraging personal initiative and cooperation among the farmers in order to improve living conditions in the countryside. These activities of the Chamber apply to all branches ot agricultural production. And, of course, in representing the interests of farmers and agricultural labourers, the Chamber acts in consonance with the interests of the other sections of the population.

title: Changes in Rural Culture
text: In respect of rural culture, it should be remembered, to begin with, that the area of cultivated land in Latvia diminished by 27% during the war. But in the very first few years of independence the area of arable land, which is one of the principal forms of rural culture, began to grow again. In 1923 it readied 1,698,425 hectares or 27.89% of the total area of agricultural and forest land. In 1929 the arable acreage covered 1,947,876 hectares or 31.46%, and in 1935 — 2,113,684 hectares or 33.85%. Compared with the pre-war acreage, the cultivated area in 1935 showed an increase of 136,603 hectares and comprised 60.39% of the total area of agricultural and forest land. The acreage of agriculturally unproductive land has been gradually diminished. And so. parallel to the process of revival in other branches, the agricultural exploitation of the soil has become more intensive than before the war. This offers the most convincing answer to the question heard so often, as to whether the agrarian reform has impeded or enhanced a more intensive exploitation of the soil. Since the recovery of Latvian independence considerable headway has been made in replenishing the number of livestock, and especially in improving the quality of the same. The following results were achieved by 1936: cows 1,261,400 head, — horses 388,800, — sheep 1,351,600 and pigs 674,400. Particular attention has been paid to the breeding of milch cattle. As a result of the strict control exercised in stock farming, the yield of milk has been increasing from year to year and the quality of the milk has improved considerably. The working up of the milk has been placed on an industrial basis, in co-operative dairies.

title: Agricultural Labour Problem
text: MEASURES FOR ITS SOLUTION. The question of meeting the local demand for agricultural labourers is one of the main problems in the economic life of Latvia. For the employment of foreign labourers in the Latvian countryside has become a permanent feature in recent years, and so much so, that the resultant situation calls for careful attention. (Of the 200,000 agricultural labourers employed in Latvia some 40,000 are enlisted abroad for working in this country.) The lack of working hands in agriculture is closely connected with the changes which have taken place in the structure of economic life. The increasing demand for working hands may be ascribed to the following main causes: 1) the upward trend of agriculture, consequent on the enforcement of the agrarian reform and the establishment of individual farmsteads in Latgale, in place of the village strips which were a peculiarity of this province formerly; 2) the expansion of the industries which is particularly noticeable in the branches which have a natural foundation in this country and are closely connected with agricultural production; 3) the enlargement of the sowing area and the development of special branches and cultures (sugar-beet, tobacco, apiculture and poultry farming). The results which have arisen in consequence of these changes might have been adjusted in a purely mechanical manner by releasing some of the labour forces from the less essential branches of industry and directing them to the countryside. The Government deemed it expedient, however, in devising a new system of providing agricultural labour, to avoid such changes as might affect wide circles of the population too severely. It was realized that the scarcity of agricultural labourers was due to yet other, even deeper causes, and these had to be taken into consideration when deciding upon the necessary remedial measures. These causes may be characterized thus: 1) the heavy loss of the nation's vital forces during the Great War and the results of the diminished birth rate during the years of the war; 2) the difference in the standard of living of the rural and urban inhabitants, in favour of the towns. As regards the first cause, it was obvious that the most direct course leading, if not to the complete overcoming of the scarcity of agricultural labourers, then at least to a diminution of this scarcity, was to make use of modern implements and machines to replace working hands in agriculture. The Government has been pursuing this course until now, promoting the mechanisation of agricultural work by granting support and loans for acquiring machines and implements. In regard to the second cause, viz., the difference between the urban and rural standards of living, it is obvious, that the most liberal and reasonable course is to adjust this difference in the living conditions between the towns and the country parts so as to make country life more attractive for the townspeople, and at the same time induce the young generation to remain in the countryside. An investigation of the causes which attract the inhabitants townwards shows that the lack of suitable dwellings in the countryside is one of the principal reasons why the people prefer to live in the towns. The statistics show that in 1935, only 629 farms had special houses for agricultural labourers, and in 3000 farms separate rooms were reserved for the labourers in the farmers' dwelling houses. The opinion prevails, therefore, that it is possible to increase the number of permanent agricultural labourers by paying greater attention to the building of suitable dwellings for them.

title: Fund for Promoting Rationalisation
text: On one hand the increased economic activity in all branches and on the other a perceptible lack of working hands, — these are the main features of the present economic situation in Latvia, which have given rise to important problems of industrial reorganisation. In this work of reorganisation the greatest importance attaches indubitably to the practical arrangement of the process of production itself, utilising all the facilities which may be obtained from modern technic. But the modernisation of technical equipment involves rather heavy expenditure, and only very few enterprises have reserved the means necessary for this purpose. Consequently, it is to be expected that many enterprises will require larger or smaller credits or other forms of support for renewing their used equipment or for modernising their plant. With a view to precluding the possibility of a high rate of interest impeding the use of credits, the Minister of Finance deemed it essential to establish a special fund, the purpose of which would be, first of all, to cover a part of the interest on loans granted to enterprises for rationalisation requirements, as well as to issue nonrepayable support. The law relating to the rationalisation fund was passed by the Cabinet on May 2, 1939. The purpose of the fund is to support all practical mechanisation and rationalisation efforts in the industrial field, as well as in other branches of economic life, paying particular attention to promoting the development of the so called natural industries, i. c. those which have a natural foundation in this country. The tasks of the fund have to be carried out in conformity with the interests of State economy and defence, as well as the general interests of the whole community. In fulfilment of the tasks outlined above, the rationalisation fund may grant non-repayable support for the following purposes: 1) for the building activities and reorganisation of the industries or other branches of economic life; 2) for acquiring new modern machines and tools; 3) for rationalising the technical, commercial and administrative organisation; 4) for consulting local and foreign experts; 5) for making investigations into the possibility of rationalising and mechanising separate branches of Latvian economic life, and, in general, enhancing the solution of other questions connected with rationalisation and mechanisation. The resources of the fund may also be used for seeking and examining new branches of industry, investigating new forms of production and new methods of research work with a view to finding the most rational means of production.

title: Latvia's Economic Position Portrayed by the President of the LCCI
text: The autumn plenary meeting of the Latvian Chamber of Commerce and Industry took place in Congress House, Riga, on November 29, 1939. The meeting was attended by the members of the Chamber and representatives of the merchants', manufacturers' and houseowners' societies, which are subordinate to the Chamber. Many high officials of State institutions were also present. The assembly passed the Chamber's budget for 1940, and listened to a report on the economic situation by the president of the Chamber, Director Andrejs Berzins, who made the following observations in the course of his address: "The European war, which has been raging already for three months, has literally gone past us, and for this we must thank God, the Leader of our nation and our own diligent people. This country has remained neutral in the present war. In the last Great War, the methods of warfare were such that by remaining neutral a country had vast opportunities for enrichment at the expense of the warring nations. But this is no longer the case, and nowadays the hardships engendered by war affect the neutral countries in equal measure." The president of the Chamber then dwelt at greater length on the events which had affected the economic interests of Latvia, mentioning in the first place the repatriation of the Baltic Germans. "The repatriation of Latvian citizens of German nationality to Germany has dealt our national economic organism a serious blow", said the speaker. "In the course of the .past five years, the programme of work drawn up for our regenerated State was based on the reserves of labour, skilled and otherwise, which were available on the spot. But now thousands of working hands have been lost to Latvia at a single stroke. And moreover they were skilled hands. According to the data compiled in 1935, there were approximately 62,000 citizens of German nationality in Latvia. About 30,000 of them were engaged in various fields of productive work. More than one-half of the working citizens of German nationality were employed in industry, commerce and communications. But it is gratifying to know that just during the last five years, the Latvians have done much to capacitate themselves for work in the branches which suffer most in consequence of the departure of the repatriated Germans. "Another problem which arises out of the repatriation of the Germans is the efflux of capital, in the form of movable property as well as in cash. Desirous of meeting the wishes of the German Reich, the Latvian Government agreed to the emigration of the German inhabitants, but this consent should by no means be construed as Implying Latvia's agreement to the exportation of the capital belonging to these German citizens, for it should be borne in mind that this capital is part of the substance of Latvia's economic organism. Repatriation of this capital would be tantamount to a transfer of the substance of our economic organism, and this is a claim which, under the prevailing circumstances, cannot be made upon Latvian national economy, nor would we be in a position to satisfy it. If all other countries have placed severe restrictions on the exportation of capital, we are all the more justified in resorting to such restrictions and interdicts, taking into consideration the specific nature of the capital involved in this particular case. This is an important issue in the entire complex of questions concerning the property of the Germans. The agreement concluded on October 30, 1939, provides for the discussion of matters connected with the repatriation of this capital at a later date. This means that there is still time to deal thoroughly with the entire complex of these problems, in order to solve them with justice and fairness, but above all, in a really practicable manner." In the further course of his speech, the president of the Chamber referred to the various conjunctural changes which have taken place in consequence of the European war. "The difficulties caused by the European war", said he, "are most keenly felt in the branches of production and activity which our Chamber represents, viz., trade, industry, shipping and real estate. The main problem which confronts us is the lack of basic materials. This deficiency arises out of the transport difficulties caused by the war. Theoretically, Latvia's trade with West Europe ought not to be impeded, as this is a neutral country. In reality, however, this trade has been almost completely suspended in consequence of naval warfare and blockade. This applies not only to the technical difficulties in importing basic materials, but in equal measure to the transport of Latvian export goods.
